afcat-r-syllogism:
CH.8 — SYLLOGISM (VERBAL) — MASTER REVISION GUIDE

📌 EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW & FOUNDATIONAL CONCEPTS

Syllogism is a deductive argument consisting of exactly three categorical propositions: two premises and one conclusion. The classic form was codified by Aristotle in his treatise Prior Analytics (c. 350 BCE) and later formalised by George Boole (1854) and the Port-Royal Logic (1662).

Each categorical proposition belongs to one of the four Standard Forms (the “A‑E‑I‑O” system):

  • A (Universal‑Affirmative): “All A are B.” – Definite, universal, affirmative.
  • E (Universal‑Negative): “No A are B.” – Definite, universal, negative.
  • I (Particular‑Affirmative): “Some A are B.” – Indefinite, particular, affirmative.
  • O (Particular‑Negative): “Some A are not B.” – Indefinite, particular, negative.

Key logical notions:

  • Distribution: A term is distributed if the proposition says something about all members of that class. In A‑propositions the subject is distributed; in E‑propositions both subject and predicate are distributed; in I‑propositions none are distributed; in O‑propositions only the predicate is distributed.
  • Quality: Whether the proposition is affirmative (A, I) or negative (E, O).
  • Quantity: Whether the proposition is universal (A, E) or particular (I, O).
  • Figure: Determined by the position of the middle term (M) in the premises. There are four figures:
    • Figure 1: M‑P (major), S‑M (minor)
    • Figure 2: P‑M (major), S‑M (minor)
    • Figure 3: M‑P (major), M‑S (minor)
    • Figure 4: P‑M (major), M‑S (minor)
  • Mood: The sequence of proposition types (e.g., AAA, EAE, AII) that, together with the figure, uniquely identifies a syllogism.

Fundamental Rules of Validity (applicable to all figures):

  1. Rule of Distribution: The middle term must be distributed in at least one premise.
  2. Rule of Undistributed Middle: The middle term must not be undistributed in both premises.
  3. Rule of Exclusive Premises: Two negative premises are forbidden.
  4. Rule of Negative Conclusion: If one premise is negative, the conclusion must be negative, and vice‑versa.
  5. Rule of Particular Premise: If a premise is particular, the conclusion must be particular.
  6. Rule of Illicit Process: No term may be distributed in the conclusion unless it is also distributed in the premise(s) where it occurs.

Three classical transformations aid in testing validity:

  • Conversion (valid for E and I; partial for A → “Some B are A”).
  • Obversion (always valid): Change quality and replace predicate with its complement.
  • Contraposition (valid for A and O; partial for E → “Some non‑B are non‑A”).

Modern exam‑oriented approach: treat every premise as true irrespective of real‑world knowledge; focus on logical form, not content.

CHALCOLITHIC AGE — MASTER REVISION GUIDE

📌 EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW & FOUNDATIONAL CONCEPTS

The Chalcolithic Age (also called the Copper‑Stone Age) marks the transitional phase between the Neolithic (purely lithic) and the fully Bronze Age societies. It is characterised by the simultaneous exploitation of copper alongside traditional stone implements, hence the term “chalco‑lithic” (Greek chalkos = copper, lithos = stone).

Chronologically, the Indian sub‑continent witnessed the Chalcolithic between c. 3000 BCE and 1500 BCE, with regional offsets:

  • West Indian Chalcolithic (Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan): c. 2500‑1500 BCE.
  • South Indian Chalcolithic (Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh): c. 2000‑1200 BCE.
  • East Indian Chalcolithic (Bengal, Odisha, Assam): c. 1800‑1000 BCE.

Key technological hallmarks:

  • Copper extraction via reduction of copper oxides in open‑air furnaces. The fundamental reaction is:
    Cu₂O + CO → 2Cu + CO₂ (operating temperature ≈ 1085 °C, the melting point of copper).
  • Co‑existence of stone tools (e.g., polished axes, grinding stones) with copper artefacts (awls, chisels, simple daggers).
  • Introduction of metal‑working waste (slag, crucibles) in archaeological layers, providing a direct proxy for metallurgical activity.

Socio‑economic fabric:

  • Predominantly rural agrarian communities practising mixed farming (wheat, barley, millets) and animal husbandry (cattle, sheep, goats).
  • Settlement architecture remained thatched‑roofed, mud‑brick or wattle‑and‑daub dwellings; burnt bricks appear only in later phases.
  • Burial customs diverge regionally: Fractional burial (West), Complete Extended burial (South), and cist‑type pit burials with grave goods (East).

DEFENCE ORGANISATIONS, WEAPONS & AGREEMENTS — MASTER REVISION GUIDE

📌 EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW & FOUNDATIONAL CONCEPTS

The Indian defence architecture is a layered, inter‑operable system built on three constitutional pillars – the Union Ministry of Defence (MoD), the three service branches (Indian Army, Indian Navy, Indian Air Force) and the Paramilitary & Coast Guard forces. Its legal backbone is the Constitution of India (Articles 53, 54, 55, 56) which vests the command of the armed forces in the President, exercised through the Council of Ministers. The MoD is subdivided into the Department of Defence Production, Department of Defence Research & Development, and Department of Ex-Servicemen Welfare, each governed by specific statutes (e.g., the Defence Production Act, 1999, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) Act, 1958).

Strategic Doctrine: India follows a “Credible Minimum Deterrence” posture for nuclear weapons (as per the 2003 Nuclear Doctrine) and a “Integrated Defence Services (IDS)” concept for conventional forces, which mandates jointness at the operational, tactical and strategic levels. The doctrine is operationalised through tri‑service exercises such as Exercise TROPEX (Theatre Level Operational Exercise – Navy’s flagship maritime joint exercise) and Exercise SAMYUKT VIMOCHAN (annual joint HADR exercise led by the Army).

Weapons Classification is anchored on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) and the Indian Arms Act, 1959. The categories are:

  • Strategic Systems – ICBMs, SLBMs, nuclear warheads, space‑based assets.
  • Operational‑Level Systems – Main battle tanks (e.g., Arjun Mk‑II), fighter aircraft (e.g., Su‑30MKI), submarines (e.g., Scorpène class), surface combatants (e.g., Kolkata class).

CH.11 — FIGURE ANALOGY (NON-VERBAL) — MASTER REVISION GUIDE

📌 EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW & FOUNDATIONAL CONCEPTS

Figure Analogy (also termed Non‑Verbal Analogy) is a staple of the logical‑reasoning segment in UPSC‑CDS, NDA and AFCAT examinations. The candidate is presented with a source pair of figures (A : B) and must select, from four or five options, the figure that completes the analogous relationship with a third figure (C : ?). The underlying cognitive process is a two‑step transformation: recognition of the rule governing the first pair, followed by application of the same rule to the third figure.

The rule‑set can be categorised into four macro‑domains:

  • Geometric Transformation: rotation, reflection, translation, scaling, and inversion.
  • Elemental Substitution: colour change, shape replacement, addition/removal of sub‑elements, or change in line‑type (solid ↔ dashed).
  • Numerical Manipulation: increment/decrement of count, arithmetic progression of angles, or systematic alteration of side‑length ratios.
  • Composite Operations: simultaneous application of two or more elementary rules (e.g., rotate 90° + replace triangle with circle).

Mastery demands fluency with the following formal definitions:

  • Rotation (θ): a rigid motion about a fixed centre O through an angle θ measured in degrees (clockwise negative, anticlockwise positive). In figure‑analogy problems, θ is almost always a multiple of 45°, 90°, or 180°.
  • Reflection (σ): a mirror operation across a line (axis) L. The axis may be horizontal, vertical, or diagonal (45°). The reflected image preserves size but reverses orientation.
  • Scaling (k): uniform enlargement or reduction by a factor k (k > 1 for enlargement, 0 < k < 1 for reduction). In most AFCAT items, k is 2 or ½.
  • Element Count (N): the total number of discrete sub‑figures (e.g., dots, triangles) present. Transformations often follow arithmetic sequences: N₂ = N₁ ± Δ, where Δ ∈ {1,2,3}.
  • Colour/Pattern Mapping (C): a bijective mapping between colour sets {red, blue, green, …} or pattern sets {solid, dashed, dotted}. The mapping is usually cyclic (e.g., red → blue → green → red).

📌 EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW & FOUNDATIONAL CONCEPTS

Pollution is the introduction of foreign undesirable substances (pollutants) into a natural medium (air, water, soil) in concentrations that cause adverse effects on ecosystems, human health, or the economy. The Pollutant may be a chemical (e.g., SO2, NOx, heavy metals), a physical entity (particulate matter, noise, radiation), or a biological agent (pathogens, invasive species).

Air Pollution – Presence of contaminants released by anthropogenic activities (combustion of fossil fuels, industrial processes, vehicular emissions) that alter the chemical composition of the troposphere. Key metrics:

  • PM2.5 & PM10: mass concentration (µg m⁻³). WHO 2021 guideline: PM2.5 ≤ 5 µg m⁻³ (annual).
  • SO₂: measured in ppb; National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS) for India – 80 ppb (24‑hr).
  • NOₓ (NO + NO₂): NAAQS – 80 ppb (24‑hr).
  • O₃: Peak 8‑hr average ≤ 70 ppb.

Water Pollution – Addition of foreign materials (organic, inorganic, thermal, radioactive) to water bodies, violating the World Health Organization (WHO) definition: “Water pollution occurs when foreign materials either from natural or other sources are added to water supplies and may be harmful to living organisms.” Critical parameters:

  • Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) – mg L⁻¹; Indian Standard for untreated sewage: ≤ 300 mg L⁻¹.
  • Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) – mg L⁻¹; typical permissible limit for industrial effluent: ≤ 250 mg L⁻¹.
  • Fecal coliform count – NMP/100 mL; safe drinking water: ≤ 0.
  • pH range – 6.5–8.5 for potable water.

Soil Pollution – Accumulation of hazardous chemicals (pesticides, heavy metals, petroleum hydrocarbons) beyond the soil’s natural buffering capacity. Key indices:

  • Enrichment Factor (EF) = (Cmetal/Creference)sample ÷ (Cmetal/Creference)background.
  • Geo‑accumulation Index (Igeo) = log₂[(Cn / 1.5 Bn)], where Cn is measured concentration and Bn is background concentration.

Legislative Framework (India)

  • Air (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 – Provides for the establishment of Central and State Pollution Control Boards (CPCB & SPCB).
  • Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 – Empowers CPCB to set standards for effluent discharge.
  • Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – Umbrella legislation; includes provisions for hazardous waste (Hazardous Waste (Management, Handling and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016).
  • National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 – Specialized adjudicatory body for environmental disputes.
  • National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) – Launched 2019; target 20‑30 % reduction in PM₂.₅ by 2024 (relative to 2017 levels).

WILDLIFE PROTECTION & CONSERVATION PROJECTS — MASTER REVISION GUIDE

📌 EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW & FOUNDATIONAL CONCEPTS

Wildlife Conservation is the practice of protecting species, their habitats, and ecosystems from excessive exploitation, habitat loss, and other anthropogenic pressures. In the Indian context, the legal backbone is the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (WP Act), which created the framework for protected areas, schedules of protected species, and the authority of the National Board for Wildlife (NBWL).

The WP Act defines a “protected area” (Section 3) as any area notified under the Act for the purpose of protecting wildlife, including national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, conservation reserves, and community reserves. The Act also introduced Schedules I‑VI that list species based on conservation priority; Schedule I includes the Indian tiger (Panthera tigris tigris), Indian elephant (Elephas maximus indicus), and the Indian rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis).

Key ecological concepts underpinning project design:

  • Carrying Capacity (K) – the maximum sustainable population size an ecosystem can support. Modeled by the logistic growth equation:
    dN/dt = rN (1 – N/K) where r = intrinsic rate of increase, N = population size.
  • Population Viability Analysis (PVA) – a stochastic simulation that estimates extinction risk over a defined horizon using parameters such as r, variance in survival, and catastrophic events.
  • Metapopulation Dynamics – the balance between local extinctions and recolonisations across habitat patches; quantified by the Levins model: dP/dt = cP(1‑P) – eP where P = proportion of occupied patches, c = colonisation rate, e = extinction rate.
  • Habitat Connectivity – measured using the cost‑distance algorithm in GIS; the least‑cost path (LCP) between two core habitats is derived from: LCP = Σ (cost_i × distance_i).

Conservation projects in India are typically multi‑agency (MoEFCC, State Forest Departments, NGOs, and the Armed Forces) and funded through a mix of central allocations, state budgets, and international grants (e.g., Global Environment Facility, GEF).

afcat-r-assumptions:
CH.10 — STATEMENTS AND ASSUMPTIONS (VERBAL) — MASTER REVISION GUIDE

📌 EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW & FOUNDATIONAL CONCEPTS

In the verbal ability segment of UPSC‑CDS, NDA and AFCAT, Statements‑and‑Assumptions (S‑A) questions test a candidate’s ability to discern logical relationships between a given statement (the premise) and a set of assumptions (implicit propositions). An assumption is a proposition that must be true for the statement to hold, yet it is not explicitly mentioned. The classic definition (as per the Oxford Dictionary of English Grammar, 3rd ed., 2015) is:

“An assumption is a necessary, unstated premise that underlies a given assertion.”

The logical scaffolding of S‑A questions rests on three pillars:

  • Necessity – The assumption must be indispensable; without it the statement collapses.
  • Sufficiency – The assumption alone does not prove the statement; it merely supports it.
  • Non‑contradiction – The assumption must not contradict any part of the statement.

Key distinctions:

  • Statement vs. Inference: An inference is a logical conclusion that can be drawn from the statement; it may be true but is not mandatory. An assumption, by contrast, is a pre‑condition.
  • Assumption vs. Implication: An implication is a conditional relationship (if‑then) explicitly or implicitly embedded; an assumption is the hidden “must‑be‑true” clause that validates the conditional.
  • Assumption vs. Reason: A reason explains why the statement is true; an assumption is a silent prerequisite.

The standard test‑taking algorithm (often abbreviated as “S‑A‑C‑R”) is:

  1. State the exact meaning of the statement in your own words.
  2. Analyze each option for necessity – ask “If this were false, would the statement still hold?”
  3. Cross‑check for contradictions with any part of the statement.
  4. Reject any option that is merely a possible inference, a general truth, or an opinion.

env-treaties:
CLIMATE CHANGE TREATIES & INDIA'S NDCS — MASTER REVISION GUIDE

📌 EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW & FOUNDATIONAL CONCEPTS

Climate Change is the long‑term alteration of temperature and typical weather patterns in a place. The scientific basis rests on the radiative forcing equation:

ΔF = α·ln(C/C₀)
where ΔF = radiative forcing (W·m⁻²), α ≈ 5.35 (IPCC AR5), C = atmospheric CO₂ concentration, C₀ = pre‑industrial CO₂ (≈280 ppm).

The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) (adopted 9 May 1992, entered into force 21 Mar 1994) provides the legal umbrella for all subsequent protocols. Its core obligations are:

  • Stabilisation of greenhouse‑gas (GHG) concentrations at a level that prevents “dangerous anthropogenic interference” with the climate system (Article 2).
  • Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) – the “bottom‑up” pledges each Party submits, reviewed every 5 years (Article 4.2).
  • Common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR) – developed nations bear historic responsibility, while developing nations receive flexibility (Article 3).

Kyoto Protocol (adopted 11 Dec 1997, entered into force 16 Feb 2005) operationalised the UNFCCC by imposing legally binding emission‑reduction targets on Annex I (industrialised) Parties. Key mechanisms:

  • Joint Implementation (JI) – Project‑based emission reductions between Annex I Parties.
  • Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) – Emission‑reduction projects in non‑Annex I Parties earning Certified Emission Reductions (CERs).
  • International Emissions Trading (IET) – Transfer of Assigned Amount Units (AAUs) among Annex I Parties.

Paris Agreement (adopted 12 Dec 2015, entered into force 4 Nov 2016) shifted from top‑down targets to a universal, bottom‑up architecture:

  • Every Party must submit an NDC every 5 years, each successive NDC must be “more ambitious” (Article 4.3).
  • Global stock‑take (GST) every 5 years to assess collective progress (Article 14).
  • Financial goal: US$100 bn/yr by 2020, scaling up to US$100 bn+ by 2025 (Article 9).
  • Transparency Framework – Common reporting format, technical expert review, facilitative multilateral consideration (Article 13).

India’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) (submitted 1 Oct 2015, updated 2022) are anchored in three pillars:

  1. Mitigation – Reduce emissions intensity of GDP by 33‑35 % by 2030 (relative to 2005) and achieve 450 GW renewable electricity capacity by 2030.
  2. Adaptation – Create a National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change (NAFCC) of ₹10,000 crore, and develop a State Action Plan on Climate Change (SAPCC) for all states.
  3. Finance & Technology Transfer – Mobilise US$10 bn annually by 2025 for climate‑resilient infrastructure.

India’s NDCs are also linked to the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC, 2008) and the India Climate Change Strategy (ICCS, 2021), which embed sector‑wise missions (e.g., National Solar Mission, National Water Mission).

Joint Military Exercise – a structured, time‑bound, multilateral or bilateral training activity wherein two or more armed forces conduct coordinated operations to achieve predefined objectives such as interoperability, doctrinal harmonisation, and strategic signalling. BRITISH EXPANSION — MASTER REVISION GUIDE

📌 EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW & FOUNDATIONAL CONCEPTS

The British expansion in the Indian sub‑continent (c. 1757‑1858) was a systematic, multi‑layered process that combined military conquest, political subjugation, and economic restructuring. It rested on three inter‑locking pillars:

  1. Military Supremacy – decisive victories in the Anglo‑Mysore, Anglo‑Maratha and Anglo‑Sikh wars, underpinned by superior artillery (e.g., 6‑pounder field guns) and disciplined infantry formations (the “line” and “column” tactics). The British also institutionalised the Regulation of the Army (1764) which standardized drill, logistics and supply chains.
  2. Political Instruments – the Subsidiary Alliance (1798) (Lord Wellesley), the Doctrine of Lapse (1848) (Lord Dalhousie), and a series of Press Acts (Censorship Act 1799, 1800, 1802) that curtailed native dissent and legitimised annexations.
  3. Economic Re‑orientation – the imposition of the Permanent Settlement (1793), the Ryotwari System (1820‑30s), and the establishment of the East India Company’s monopoly over customs, opium, and salt. These policies generated a fiscal surplus that financed further wars and administrative reforms.

Key Definitions:

  • Subsidiary Alliance: A treaty whereby an Indian ruler accepted a permanent British garrison, paid for its upkeep, and surrendered the right to conduct independent foreign policy.
  • Doctrine of Lapse: A legal doctrine stating that a princely state without a natural heir would “lapse” to the Crown, irrespective of adopted heirs.
  • Annexation: The formal incorporation of a sovereign territory into British India, usually ratified by a proclamation and a subsequent Act of Parliament (e.g., the Punjab Annexation Act, 1849).
  • Press Acts (1799‑1802): A series of statutes that empowered the Governor‑General to censor newspapers, confiscate seditious pamphlets, and imprison editors without trial.

MAGADHA EXPANSION — MASTER REVISION GUIDE

📌 EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW & FOUNDATIONAL CONCEPTS

The Magadha Empire (c. 6th century BC – c. 185 BC) evolved from a modest Mahājanapada into the pre‑eminent power of ancient India, laying the political, economic, and cultural foundations for the Mauryan and post‑Mauryan world. Its expansion can be dissected into four dynastic phases:

  1. Haryanka Dynasty (c. 544–413 BC) – founded by Bimbisāra (c. 543–491 BC) and consolidated by Ajātasattu (c. 491–460 BC). Core strategy: diplomatic marriage alliances (e.g., Bimbisāra‑Vajira of Vesālī) and systematic annexation of neighbouring Mahājanapadas (Anga, Vatsa, Kashi).
  2. Shishunaga Dynasty (c. 413–345 BC) – a usurper‑king from the Shudra class, who shifted the capital to Rajagriha and later to Pataliputra. Notable for the first recorded use of a standing army of 10,000 infantry + 1,000 cavalry as per the Mahāvaṃśa inscription.
  3. Nanda Dynasty (c. 345–322 BC) – founded by Mahāpaṇḍa Nanda. The Nandas introduced a centralized revenue system based on the kṣetra‑pātra (land‑assessment) model, levying a uniform tax of 1/6th of agricultural produce. Their army allegedly numbered 1,200,000 (including 9,000 war‑elephants), a figure corroborated by the Arthashastra (Kautilya, 3rd century BC).
  4. Maurya Dynasty (c. 322–185 BC) – inaugurated by Chandragupta Maurya (322–298 BC) after overthrowing Dhana‑Nanda. The Mauryan period witnessed the apex of Magadhan expansion, culminating under Āśoka the Great (268–232 BC) with the annexation of the entire Indian subcontinent (except the far south). The Mauryan administration codified the Arthashastra principles: a bureaucratic hierarchy of 10 viceroyalties (Uparikas), a spy‑network (Gupta‑Sainya), and a standardized weight‑measure system (1 rati = 0.11 g).

Key Geophysical Drivers:

  • Strategic Location: The Ganges‑Yamuna floodplain offered fertile alluvial soil (average yield ≈ 1.2 t/ha) and a natural highway for riverine trade.
  • Iron Ore Deposits in the Vindhyan foothills enabled mass production of steel‑tempered swords (Wootz steel, carbon content 1.2‑1.5 %).
  • Monsoon‑Driven Agriculture: Predictable 4‑month monsoon allowed two‑crop cycles, supporting a standing army of > 1 million without fiscal collapse.

CORE ECONOMIC CONCEPTS & SECTORS — MASTER REVISION GUIDE

📌 EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW & FOUNDATIONAL CONCEPTS

Economics is the systematic study of how societies allocate scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants. The discipline bifurcates into micro‑economics (individual agents, markets, price formation) and macroeconomics (aggregate variables, national income, inflation, unemployment).

Scarcity (the axiom of economics) implies that the marginal benefit of a good must be weighed against its opportunity cost—the value of the next best alternative foregone. The principle of marginal analysis (Samuelson, 1947) dictates that rational agents act until marginal benefit = marginal cost.

The Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) graphically represents the maximum feasible output combinations of two goods given fixed technology and resources. Points on the frontier denote efficient production; points inside indicate inefficiency; points outside are unattainable without economic growth.

Key macro‑economic aggregates:

  • Gross Domestic Product (GDP) – market value of all final goods & services produced within a country’s borders in a given period.
    Expenditure approach: GDP = C + I + G + (X – M) where C = consumption, I = investment, G = government spending, X = exports, M = imports.
  • Gross National Product (GNP) – GDP plus net factor income from abroad.
  • National Income (NI) – sum of all factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) earned by residents.
  • Inflation – sustained rise in the general price level, measured by Consumer Price Index (CPI) or Wholesale Price Index (WPI). The Quantity Theory of Money (Fisher, 1911) expresses it as MV = PT.
  • Unemployment – classified as frictional, structural, cyclical, and seasonal; measured by the Unemployment Rate = (Unemployed / Labour Force) × 100.

Core policy instruments:

  • Fiscal Policy – government’s use of taxation and expenditure to influence aggregate demand. The Keynesian multiplier (k = 1 / (1 – MPC)) quantifies the impact of a change in autonomous spending.
  • Monetary Policy – central bank’s control of money supply and interest rates. The Liquidity Preference Theory (Keynes, 1936) links money demand to income and interest rates.
  • Balance of Payments (BoP) – systematic record of all economic transactions with the rest of the world, comprising the Current Account, Capital Account, and Financial Account.
